title: Overview
summary: What a fitter config is, and the four pieces every config is built from.
body:
Fitter is a declarative language for pulling structured data out of web pages, JSON/XML APIs, PDFs and more — then reshaping it into exactly the object or array you want. You write a config (JSON or YAML); fitter runs it and returns the result. No code to write per source.

Every config passed to `fitter_run` / the CLI / this playground is a **CliItem**:

```json
{
  "item": { "connector_config": { }, "model": { } },
  "limits": { },
  "references": { }
}
```

- **item.connector_config** — where the raw data comes from (HTTP, a static value, a generated sequence, a cached reference, a local file, a headless browser, a plugin...) and how to parse its body (json / HTML / XML / xpath / pdf). See [Connectors](#/docs/connectors) and [Parsers](#/docs/parsers).
- **item.model** — what to extract from the parsed body: a single scalar, an object, or an array, built from [Fields](#/docs/model-fields) whose paths are written in the selector language of the chosen parser.
- **limits** — optional throttling (max parallel requests per host, max concurrent browser instances). See [Limits](#/docs/limits).
- **references** — optional named values prefetched once and reused across the config, e.g. an auth token or a shared lookup list. See [References & caching](#/docs/references).

On top of the base value, any field can be swapped for a **generated value** (computed instead of extracted — an expression, a template, a nested fetch, a random uuid...) and can carry a **condition** that omits it from the output when false. See [Generated values](#/docs/generated-values) and [Conditions](#/docs/conditions).

> This playground compiles the real fitter engine (the same Go code behind the CLI and MCP server) to WebAssembly and runs it entirely in your browser — every result you see here is a real run, not a canned demo. Two things don't work in-browser and need the native binary: headless-browser connectors (`browser_config`) and anything touching the local filesystem or native plugins (`file_config`, `plugin_connector_config`) — both are called out where relevant.

Head to [the Playground](#/playground) to try it, or [Examples](#/examples) for a runnable gallery of every feature below.

title: Connectors
summary: Where the raw data comes from: HTTP, static values, sequences, references, files, headless browsers, plugins.
body:
`item.connector_config` decides where the bytes to parse come from, and `response_type` decides how to parse them (see [Parsers](#/docs/parsers)). Exactly one connector kind is set per `connector_config`:

```json
{
  "response_type": "json",
  "attempts": 3,
  "null_on_error": false,
  "server_config": { }
}
```

- `attempts` — optional retry count.
- `null_on_error` — return `null` for this field/branch instead of failing the whole run (very useful on optional nested fetches).

### server_config — HTTP(S) requests

```json
"server_config": {
  "method": "GET",
  "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {{{RefName=Token}}}" },
  "timeout": 30,
  "body": "",
  "json_raw_body": {},
  "proxy": { "server": "http://host:3128", "username": "", "password": "" },
  "oauth2": { "token_url": "https://.../token", "grant_type": "client_credentials" }
}
```

`url` (on the parent `connector_config`) and `headers`/`body` all support [placeholders](#/docs/placeholders). `oauth2` fetches/refreshes/caches a token automatically and sends it as the `Authorization` header — works for `client_credentials` and `refresh_token` grants, with `token_file` persisting rotated refresh tokens between runs (native CLI/server only, since it writes to disk).

In the browser playground, requests go out as real `fetch()` calls — only CORS-friendly APIs work (GitHub, OpenLibrary, CoinGecko, Hacker News Algolia, httpbin...). Arbitrary page scraping usually needs either a CORS proxy or the native binary, since the target site controls CORS headers, not fitter.

### static_config — an inline value

```json
"static_config": { "value": "{\"name\": \"fitter\"}" }
```
Parses a literal string you provide instead of fetching anything — handy for tests, fixtures, and offline demos. `raw` accepts already-structured JSON instead of a string.

### int_sequence_config — generate a range, no network

```json
"int_sequence_config": { "start": 1, "end": 10, "step": 1 }
```
Produces `[start, end)` like `range()`. Combine with `root_path: "@this"` and a per-item `generated.model` to drive pagination — one nested fetch per page number.

### reference_config — read a prefetched reference

```json
"reference_config": { "name": "MyRef" }
```
Uses a value already fetched under the top-level `references` map (see [References & caching](#/docs/references)) as this item's own source, instead of fetching again.

### file_config — local file (native-only in this playground)

```json
"file_config": { "path": "/path/to/file", "use_formatting": false }
```
Reads a local file's content. `use_formatting` runs [placeholders](#/docs/placeholders) over the file content after reading. **Doesn't work in the browser build** — there's no real local filesystem inside the WASM sandbox. See the [file_config example](#/examples/file-connector-native-only) for a full config (viewable/copyable in the Playground, Run stays disabled) — use the native `fitter_cli` or MCP server to actually run it.

### plugin_connector_config — custom Go plugin (native-only)

```json
"plugin_connector_config": { "name": "my_plugin", "config": { } }
```
Loads a compiled `.so` plugin (via `FITTER_PLUGINS`) implementing fitter's connector interface. Go's native plugin loader isn't available under `GOOS=js` at all, so this **only runs on the native binary**. See the [plugin connector example](#/examples/plugin-connector-native-only) (also covers `generated.plugin`, the computed-field form).

### browser_config — headless browser (native-only)

```json
"browser_config": {
  "playwright": { "browser": "Chromium", "install": true, "timeout": 30, "wait": 30, "type_of_wait": "networkidle", "stealth": false, "storage_state_file": "" },
  "chromium": { "path": "/path/to/chromium", "timeout": 30, "wait": 10000, "flags": [] },
  "docker":   { "image": "docker.io/zenika/alpine-chrome:with-node", "entry_point": "chromium-browser", "timeout": 30, "wait": 10000 }
}
```
Renders JS-heavy pages with a real browser before parsing — needed for SPAs, login-gated pages (`storage_state_file`, created once via `fitter_cli browser-login`), or anti-bot pages (`stealth`). Requires an actual OS process (a browser, or Docker), so **it's stubbed out of the WebAssembly build**: `pkg/connectors/browser_js.go` returns a clear "not supported in the WebAssembly build" error for every call. See the [browser connectors example](#/examples/browser-config-native-only) for a full config — it opens in the Playground for inspection/copying, but Run stays disabled there; use the native `fitter_cli`/MCP server for real browser automation. Pair with `limits.playwright_instance` / `chromium_instance` / `docker_containers` to cap concurrency.

title: Parsers (response_type)
summary: json, HTML, XML, xpath, pdf — and the selector language each one expects in field paths.
body:
`connector_config.response_type` picks both the parser and the selector language used by every `path` inside `model` for that item (paths are relative once you're inside an array's `root_path`):

- **`json`** — [gjson](https://github.com/tidwall/gjson) paths: `"data.items.0.name"`, `"products.#.title"`, `"@this"` (the whole current node), `"@this|@keys"`. See the [Static JSON example](#/examples/static-json).
- **`HTML`** — goquery / CSS selectors: `"div.article > a"`. Add `"html_attribute": "href"` on a `base_field` to read an attribute instead of the element's text. See the [HTML example](#/examples/html-css).
- **`XML`** — xmlquery / XPath: `"//channel/title/text()"`. See the [XML/RSS example](#/examples/xml-rss).
- **`xpath`** — also xmlquery / XPath, usable on *either* HTML or XML documents — pick this one over `HTML` when CSS selectors aren't expressive enough (e.g. `//a[contains(@class,'title')]`). See the [XPath-on-HTML example](#/examples/xpath-html).
- **`pdf`** — not a selector language: the parsed "document" exposes fixed fields (`total_pages`, `text`, ...) that you read with plain `json`-style paths on the extracted structure. See the [PDF example](#/examples/pdf-extract).

`response_type` also applies inside a nested `generated.model` fetch (it can differ from the parent's — e.g. a JSON API can drive a nested HTML page fetch) and inside `references` entries.

title: Model & fields
summary: object_config, array_config, base_field, and the Field union that ties them together.
body:
`item.model` is exactly one of:

- `"base_field"` — extract a single scalar for the whole item.
- `"object_config"` — build an object.
- `"array_config"` — build an array.

### object_config

```json
{ "fields": { "<name>": <Field>, ... }, "condition": "" }
```
Each entry in `fields` is a **Field**, which is itself a union — exactly one of:

```json
{
  "base_field": { },      // a scalar
  "object_config": { },   // a nested object
  "array_config": { },    // a nested array
  "first_of": [ <Field>, ... ]  // first non-empty alternative wins
}
```
See the [nested object+array example](#/examples/nested-object-array) and the [first_of example](#/examples/first-of-fallback). `condition` (evaluated against the source node before resolution) can omit the whole object from its parent — see [Conditions](#/docs/conditions).

### array_config

```json
{
  "root_path": "<selector of the repeating element>",
  "item_config": <ObjectConfig>,
  "length_limit": 10,
  "reverse": false,
  "condition": "",
  "item_condition": "fSrc.in_stock && fRes.price > 0",
  "static_array": { "length": 3, "items": { "0": <Field>, ... } }
}
```
`root_path` selects the repeating node; every path inside `item_config` is relative to it. `item_config` can itself be `{ "fields": {...} }` (object items) or `{ "field": <BaseField> }` (array of scalars). `item_condition` filters *built* items — see [Conditions](#/docs/conditions) and the [conditional fields example](#/examples/conditional-fields). `static_array` skips `root_path` entirely and instead gives each numeric index its own independent field — see the [static array example](#/examples/static-array).

### base_field

See [Base field types](#/docs/base-field-types) for the full `type` list, [Generated values](#/docs/generated-values) for `generated`, and [Conditions](#/docs/conditions) for `condition`.

```json
{
  "type": "string",
  "path": "<selector, relative when inside an array item>",
  "html_attribute": "href",
  "condition": "fRes > 0",
  "generated": { },
  "first_of": [ <BaseField>, ... ]
}
```
`is_array: true` on the top-level `model` forces array output even for a single-object shape — rarely needed, mostly relevant to `generated.model` fields.

title: Base field types
summary: string, int, int64, float, float64, boolean, html, raw_string, null, array, object.
body:
`base_field.type` is one of:

- `string` — trimmed, with special/control characters normalized. Use `raw_string` if you need the untouched value.
- `int`, `int64`, `float`, `float64` — numeric coercion from the parsed value.
- `boolean`
- `html` — keeps the inner HTML markup instead of just text; only meaningful when the connector's `response_type` is `HTML`.
- `raw_string` — the plain extracted value, no trimming/normalization.
- `null` — always resolves to `null` (useful as a `first_of` fallback, or a placeholder field to fill in later).
- `array` / `object` — used together with `generated.model` (a nested fetch that returns a structured value) or with a plain `path` pointing at a JSON sub-tree you want to pass through untouched (e.g. `"path": "@this"`).

See the [Generated values showcase](#/examples/generated-values-showcase) and [Reference-as-source](#/examples/reference-as-source) examples for `object`/`array` types in practice.

title: Generated values
summary: calculated, formatted, static, uuid, model (nested fetch), plugin, file, file_storage.
body:
`base_field.generated` replaces extraction with computation. Pick exactly one:

```json
{
  "calculated": { "type": "boolean", "expression": "fRes > 500" },
  "formatted":  { "template": "https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id={PL}" },
  "static":     { "type": "int", "value": "65" },
  "uuid":       { "regexp": "" },
  "model":      { "connector_config": {}, "model": {}, "type": "object" },
  "plugin":     { "name": "...", "config": {} },
  "file":       { "url": "https://host{PL}", "file_name": "", "path": "/dir" },
  "file_storage": { "content": "{PL}\n", "file_name": "out.csv", "path": "/tmp" }
}
```

- **calculated** — an [expr-lang](https://expr-lang.org/) expression evaluated with `fRes` (the extracted value, typed), `fResJson` (its JSON string form), `fResRaw` (raw bytes), and `fIndex` (index in the parent array, if any). See [Expressions](#/docs/expressions) and the [crypto top-5](#/examples/crypto-top5) / [Telegram briefing](#/examples/telegram-briefing) examples.
- **formatted** — a template string where `{PL}` is replaced with the field's current/parent value.
- **static** — a fixed value baked into the config (`value` for scalars, `raw` for structured JSON).
- **uuid** — a random UUID v4; `regexp` optionally extracts just part of it.
- **model** — the most powerful one: runs an entirely separate `connector_config`+`model` per value, with `{PL}` (or `{{{FromExp=...}}}`) injecting the parent value into its URL/body. This is how nested/joined fetches work — see [book→author join](#/examples/book-author-join), [reference-as-source](#/examples/reference-as-source), and the Telegram example's outbound POST.
- **plugin** — a custom Go plugin field (native-only, same `.so`-loading constraint as `plugin_connector_config`, see [Connectors](#/docs/connectors)).
- **file** — downloads a URL to local disk and resolves to the local path (native-only — no real filesystem in the browser build).
- **file_storage** — writes the value to a local file, optionally appending (native-only, same reason).

See the [generated values showcase](#/examples/generated-values-showcase) for `static`/`uuid`/`formatted` side by side.

title: Conditions
summary: condition, item_condition — omit fields/items instead of nulling them, using expr-lang.
body:
`base_field`, `object_config` and `array_config` all accept `condition`; `array_config` additionally accepts `item_condition`. Anything except `true` (including an evaluation error) **omits** the field/item from the output entirely — it does not produce `null`.

- **base_field.condition** — evaluated against the *extracted* value: `fRes` (typed value), `fResJson`, `fResRaw`, `fIndex`, and `fSrc` (the source node the value came from, siblings included — so you can gate a field on a sibling's value without extracting the sibling itself).
- **object_config.condition / array_config.condition** — evaluated *before* resolution, against the source node only (no `fRes` yet) — use it to skip building an entire object/array.
- **array_config.item_condition** — evaluated per *built* item: `fRes` (the built item), `fSrc` (the source element it was built from), `fIndex` (its index). This is the one for declarative array filtering — drop items by attributes on the source without extracting them into the output. Not applied to `static_array`.

See the [conditional fields example](#/examples/conditional-fields), which combines all three: `item_condition` drops out-of-stock/zero-price products, and a field-level `condition` additionally omits `discount_pct` when it isn't positive.

title: Expressions (expr-lang)
summary: The expression language behind calculated fields, conditions, notifier gates and {{{FromExp=...}}}.
body:
Wherever fitter takes an expression — `generated.calculated.expression`, `condition`/`item_condition`, `notifier_config.expression`, and the `{{{FromExp=...}}}` placeholder — it's evaluated with [expr-lang](https://expr-lang.org/), a small, fast, Go-native expression language (think a safer subset of a scripting language: arithmetic, string ops, comparisons, ternaries, `map`/`filter`, string/array builtins).

Predefined variables available in these expressions:

- `fRes` — the extracted/built value, typed (string, number, bool, map, slice depending on context).
- `fResJson` — the same value as a JSON string (handy with `fromJSON(...)` + `map`/`filter` for array reshaping).
- `fResRaw` — the value as raw bytes.
- `fIndex` — index within the parent array, where applicable.
- `fSrc` — (conditions only) the source node the value was resolved from.
- `FNull` / `FNil` / `isNull(v)` / `FNewLine` — null/newline helpers.

Common patterns seen across the examples:

```
upper(fRes) + "!"                                  // string transform
fRes > 0 ? "📈 up" : "📉 down"                       // ternary
trim(fRes[:120]) + "…"                              // slicing + concat
join(map(fromJSON(fResJson), { .title }), "\n")     // reshape a JSON array into text
```

See it in action in the [crypto top-5](#/examples/crypto-top5), [static JSON](#/examples/static-json), [HTML](#/examples/html-css) and [Telegram briefing](#/examples/telegram-briefing) examples.

title: References & caching
summary: Named values prefetched once (with optional TTL) and reused via reference_config or {{{RefName=...}}}.

title: Limits
summary: host_request_limiter and concurrency caps for browser connectors.
body:
Top-level, optional:

```json
"limits": {
  "host_request_limiter": { "example.com": 5 },
  "chromium_instance": 1,
  "docker_containers": 1,
  "playwright_instance": 1
}
```

- `host_request_limiter` caps the number of parallel in-flight requests *per host* — essential when a nested `generated.model` fires one fetch per array item against a rate-limited API. See the [book→author join example](#/examples/book-author-join) (caps `openlibrary.org` to 2 concurrent requests).
- `chromium_instance` / `docker_containers` / `playwright_instance` cap concurrent headless-browser instances of each kind — only relevant to `browser_config` (native-only, see [Connectors](#/docs/connectors)).

title: Placeholders
body:
Placeholders can appear in URLs, headers, request bodies, `formatted` templates, file paths/content, and static values:

- `{PL}` — the current/parent field value (used inside `generated.model`'s `url`/`body` and `generated.formatted.template`).
- `{INDEX}` / `{HUMAN_INDEX}` — index in the parent array, 0-based / 1-based.
- `{{{json_path}}}` — a value from the propagated object/array field, e.g. `{{{latitude}}}`.
- `{{{RefName=SomeName}}}` — the whole value of a [reference](#/docs/references); `{{{RefName=SomeName json.path}}}` extracts by path.
- `{{{FromInput=.}}}` — the `input` argument passed to the run (the tool call's input, or the playground's input box); `{{{FromInput=json.path}}}` extracts by path from it if it's JSON. See the [book search example](#/examples/book-author-join) (plain text input) and the [Telegram example](#/examples/telegram-briefing) (JSON input: token + chat_id).
- `{{{FromEnv=ENV_KEY}}}` — an environment variable (native runtimes only — the browser has no process environment).
- `{{{FromExp=fRes + 5}}}` — an [expr-lang expression](#/docs/expressions), evaluated and interpolated.
- `{{{FromFile=./file.txt}}}` — a local file's content, which may itself contain placeholders (native-only, no filesystem in the browser build).
- `{{{FromURL=http://host}}}` — the response body of a GET request, inlined.

See them combined in the [Telegram briefing example](#/examples/telegram-briefing): `{{{FromInput=token}}}` in the URL, `{{{FromInput=chat_id}}}` and `{{{FromExp=...}}}` in the body, `{{{RefName=btc usd}}}` / `{{{RefName=btc trend}}}` pulling from prefetched references.

title: Notifiers
summary: item.notifier_config — push the parsed result somewhere (Telegram, HTTP, Redis, file, console).
body:
```json
"notifier_config": {
  "expression": "len(fResRaw) > 0",
  "template": "",
  "send_array_by_item": false,
  "force": false,

  "http":         { "url": "https://hooks.example.com", "method": "POST", "headers": {}, "timeout": 30 },
  "telegram_bot": { "token": "{{{FromEnv=TG_TOKEN}}}", "users_id": [123], "pretty": true, "only_msg": false },
  "redis":        { "addr": "localhost:6379", "password": "", "db": 0, "channel": "fitter" },
  "file":         { "content": "{PL}\n", "file_name": "out.log", "path": "/tmp", "append": true },
  "console":      { "only_result": true }
}
```

The parse result is still returned by the tool call either way; the notifier *additionally* delivers it wherever configured. `expression` (expr-lang, over `fRes*`) gates whether to notify at all; `template` reshapes the payload first; `send_array_by_item` fires one notification per array element instead of one for the whole result; `force` notifies even when parsing errored.

> `notifier_config` is driven by the long-running fitter **service**/**scheduler** and by MCP tool calls that opt into notification — it is *not* invoked by the bare `fitter_run`/`ParseCtx` call this playground's WASM bridge uses, so there's no interactive notifier demo here. The [Telegram briefing example](#/examples/telegram-briefing) instead demonstrates the same idea directly, as a plain outbound HTTP call inside `generated.model` — the mechanics of building the message are identical, just wired manually instead of through `notifier_config`.

title: MCP server
summary: fitter_mcp exposes fitter_run / fitter_run_file / fitter_config_reference as MCP tools for AI agents.
body:
`fitter_mcp` runs fitter as an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server so any MCP-aware agent (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, etc.) can author and execute fitter configs on demand:

- **`fitter_run`** — run an inline config (JSON or YAML) against optional input, get the parsed result back. Best for one-off/ad-hoc extraction requests.
- **`fitter_run_file`** — run a config already saved to disk, for reusable/curated configs.
- **`fitter_config_reference`** — returns the condensed config schema reference (the same content this Docs section is derived from) so the agent can self-correct without guessing field names.

```bash
# stdio mode, spawned by the MCP client
fitter_mcp

# hosted HTTP mode
fitter_mcp --http :8080
```

Supports remote/hosted mode over streamable HTTP, a Docker image (including a Playwright-enabled variant for browser_config), OAuth2 device-flow login for API accounts, and `browser-login` for saving a real logged-in browser session (`storage_state_file`) that configs can reuse. See [Install the MCP server](#/docs/install) for exact registration commands per client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Docker), or the [README's MCP section](https://github.com/PxyUp/fitter#how-to-use-fitter_mcp) for further Docker/OAuth2 recipes, since those are environment-specific and out of scope for a browser playground.

title: Install the MCP server
summary: Register fitter_mcp in Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and other MCP clients — native binary or Docker.
body:
Fitter's MCP server (`fitter_mcp`) works with any MCP-compatible client over stdio, or over streamable HTTP for a shared/remote server. Get the binary from the [release page](https://github.com/PxyUp/fitter/releases), build it with `go build -o fitter_mcp ./cmd/mcp`, or run it via Docker — then register it below. See [MCP server](#/docs/mcp) for the tools it exposes.

### Claude Code

```bash
# native binary, registered once for every project
claude mcp add fitter -s user -- /path/to/fitter_mcp

# Docker, no local binary needed
claude mcp add fitter -s user -- docker run --rm -i ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:latest

# remote/hosted server over streamable HTTP
claude mcp add --transport http fitter http://localhost:8080/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
```

Browser configs (`browser_config`) need the `:playwright` image instead of the default slim one — see Docker images below.

### Claude Desktop

One click: download `fitter-mcp-<os>-<arch>.mcpb` from the [release page](https://github.com/PxyUp/fitter/releases) and open it — Claude Desktop installs the server automatically.

Manual registration (edit Claude Desktop's config, `claude_desktop_config.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fitter": { "command": "/path/to/fitter_mcp" }
  }
}
```

Docker instead of a local binary — point `command`/`args` at `docker` the same way as Claude Code above:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fitter": { "command": "docker", "args": ["run", "--rm", "-i", "ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:latest"] }
  }
}
```

### Cursor & other MCP clients

Any client that speaks stdio MCP accepts the same command/args shape — adapt the key names to your client's config format (Cursor's `mcp.json`, Windsurf, etc.):

```json
{
  "command": "/path/to/fitter_mcp",
  "args": []
}
```

Docker variant:

```json
{
  "command": "docker",
  "args": ["run", "--rm", "-i", "ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:latest"]
}
```

Clients that support remote/HTTP MCP servers can instead point at a hosted `fitter_mcp --http :8080` endpoint (optionally with `FITTER_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN` and a bearer header), same as the Claude Code example above.

### Docker images

Two multi-arch (`linux/amd64` + `linux/arm64`) images ship with every release:

- **`ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:latest`** — slim: just the fitter binary and CA certificates. `server_config`/`static_config`/`reference_config`/`int_sequence_config`/`file_config` connectors work; `browser_config` (Chromium/Docker/Playwright) does not.
- **`ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:playwright`** — the same image plus Chromium, Firefox and WebKit preinstalled, matched to the `playwright-go` version fitter is built against — no `"install": true` needed in configs. Use this tag whenever a config sets `connector_config.browser_config`.

```bash
docker run --rm -i ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:latest         # slim, stdio mode
docker run --rm -i ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:playwright      # with browsers, stdio mode

# hosted HTTP mode (either image)
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 \
  -e FITTER_MCP_HTTP_ADDR=:8080 -e FITTER_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN=my-secret \
  ghcr.io/pxyup/fitter-mcp:latest
```

### Official registry

Fitter publishes to the [official MCP registry](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/registry) (`io.github.PxyUp/fitter`) automatically on every release and is listed at [github.com/mcp](https://github.com/mcp) once onboarded — clients that browse the registry can discover and install it directly, without hand-writing any of the JSON above.

> All of this is native-binary/Docker territory — none of it runs inside this site's WASM playground. See [MCP server](#/docs/mcp) for what the tools do once it's registered, and [CLI & Agent](#/docs/cli) for the one-shot `fitter_cli` alternative.

title: CLI & Agent
summary: fitter_cli for one-shot runs, auth and browser-login; fitter_agent for an interactive config-building REPL.
body:
**fitter_cli** runs a config once from the command line — the native counterpart to this playground's "Run" button:

```bash
go install github.com/PxyUp/fitter/cmd/fitter_cli@latest
fitter_cli -path config.json           # or .yaml
fitter_cli -config '{"item":{...}}'    # inline
```

Two helper subcommands persist local state that in-browser configs can't (no filesystem, no OS-level browser process):

- **`fitter_cli auth`** — connects an OAuth2 account (device flow by default, works headless) and writes a `token_file` that `server_config.oauth2` configs can reuse.
- **`fitter_cli browser-login`** — opens a real browser window, lets you log in by hand, and saves the session as a `storage_state_file` for `browser_config.playwright` to replay later (cookies + optionally IndexedDB).

**fitter_agent** is an interactive REPL that helps you *build* a config for a page/API you describe in plain language, refine it turn by turn, and save the result — useful for going from "I want data from this page" to a working config faster than hand-writing paths. See the [README's Agent section](https://github.com/PxyUp/fitter#how-to-use-fitter_agent) for the full command list and an example session.

Both also power the long-running **fitter service** (`http_server` + `trigger_config`: scheduler or HTTP-triggered reruns) — out of scope for this playground, which is strictly one-shot per run.
